questions.question: Describe how Ayesha’s past as Veero is revealed in Sabiha Sumar’s Silent Waters and explain its significance.
questions.solution_html:
• Ayesha is revealed to have been Veero, a Sikh woman who survived the violence and threat of
  • sexual assault during Partition - later lives in Pakistan under a new religious identity and appears
  • to have built a settled life with her son - the past remains present through her silence, gestures and
  • memories - her son becomes influenced by religious extremism - her tragic decision to jump into
  • a well echoes the fate of women who faced unbearable pressure during Partition. Veero/Ayesha’s
  • story demonstrates that Partition trauma does not end with migration or the creation of borders - it
  • continues to shape memory, identity and later generations - it also exposes patriarchal ideas of
  • honour and the silencing of women’s experiences. [ U] / [CO1]

questions.question: Explain why Sunderlal's idealization of Lajo as a goddess becomes problematic.
questions.solution_html:
• Lajo is abducted during Partition and later recovered. Sunderlal publicly advocates that recovered
  • women should be accepted back into their families. Yet, instead of restoring an ordinary, intimate
  • relationship with Lajo, he idealises her as a goddess. This apparently respectful attitude becomes
  • problematic because it turns Lajo into a symbol of purity, sacrifice and community honour rather
  • than recognising her as a person with her own feelings and traumatic experiences – his idealisation
  • creates emotional distance and makes it difficult for Lajo to speak about what happened to her -
  • criticises patriarchal attitudes that silence women even when they are publicly honoured.
  • / [CO1]

questions.question: Explain the significance of police firing in conveying the central concern of the poem "Karachi".
questions.solution_html:
• Police firing contributes to the atmosphere of fear, violence and insecurity - shows ordinary
  • people caught in events they cannot control - highlights the human cost of political or communal
  • unrest. Alongside the images of corpses and vultures, the firing suggests a society in which death
  • and violence have entered everyday life - image criticises violence and narrow nationalism -
  • directs attention to the vulnerability and shared humanity of common people.
  • / [CO2]

questions.question: Examine the significance of the image of the entombed minaret in the poem "The Country Without a Post Office".
questions.solution_html:
• The image of an entombed minaret can be read as a sign that cultural, religious and communal life
  • has been buried or obstructed by violence. A minaret normally belongs to a living community and
  • is associated with worship and public presence; its entombment suggests the silencing of that
  • community and the destruction of familiar spaces. / [CO2]

questions.question: Interpret the significance of Garm Hawa's refusal to provide easy comfort or resolution. What does the ending reveal about the relationship between personal experience, historical trauma, and hope?
questions.solution_html:
• Partition- a continuing experience- not a closed historical event. The film avoids a simple, happy
  • resolution. Salim Mirza and his family-financial hardship, social suspicion and insecurity as
  • Muslims who remain in India after Partition. Salim is suspected and humiliated because of his
  • links with relatives in Pakistan - communal mistrust enters ordinary life - family’s decision to
  • migrate arises from accumulated pressure and disappointment - film does not offer an easy
  • solution to these problems- in the end, however, Salim encounters young people protesting for
  • justice and decides to remain in India and join their struggle - ending acknowledges continuing
  • uncertainty and injustice. - does not erase the trauma or guarantee success - offers cautious hope
  • through collective action, secular values and the possibility of rebuilding belonging - film links
  • personal suffering with larger historical forces while suggesting that people can respond through
  • resistance and civic commitment. / [CO3]

questions.question: Discuss the significance of feminist interventions in recovering the silenced experiences of Partition.
questions.solution_html:
• The essay “A Will to Say or Unsay: Female Silences and Discursive Interventions in Partition
  • Narratives” by Parvinder Mehta explores the complex relationship between silence, trauma,
  • memory and representation in narratives of the Partition of India. To develop her argument, Mehta
  • analyses a range of literary and cinematic texts that deal with Partition and its aftermath. These
  • include Rajinder Singh Bedi’s short story “Lajwanti”, Sabiha Sumar’s film Khamosh Pani (Silent
  • Waters) and Shauna Singh Baldwin’s novel What the Body Remembers. Conventional Partition
  • histories: politics, independence and migration - Marginalisation of women’s experiences -
  • Abduction, sexual violence, forced migration and loss - Patriarchy, honour and control over
  • women’s bodies - Lajwanti: Lajo’s abduction and return - Sunderlal’s public advocacy for
  • recovered women - Idealisation of Lajo as a goddess - Woman as symbol rather than individual -
  • Silence; lack of emotional intimacy and agency - Silent Waters: Veero’s transformation into
  • Ayesha - Past trauma and religious extremism - Identity, memory and patriarchal control - Silence
  • and tragic ending - What the Body Remembers: women’s bodily and domestic experiences -
  • Gendered power and communal violence - Trauma through memory, gesture and silence -
  • Recovery of marginalised voices - Silence as fear, shame, repression or resistance - Women’s
  • agency and survival - Challenge to official historical narratives - Gendered cost of Partition -
  • Women’s experiences essential to understanding Partition. / [CO1]
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Analyse the function of spatial movement in the poem "Broken Bengal". How does the continuous movement from one place to another reinforce the idea of displacement?
questions.solution_html:
• Taslima Nasrin; Partition and division of Bengal - Homeland, memory and belonging - Mangoes,
  • jackfruits, sunlight, rain and harvest festivals - Familiar landscape and cultural roots - Emotional
  • attachment to place - Forced movement and separation from home - Political division and
  • communal hostility - Uprooting and unfamiliar places - Instability, insecurity and loss - Physical
  • movement versus emotional belonging - Flower garden invaded by a wild bull - Destruction of
  • peace and harmony - Broken dreams and separated people - Land reaching towards separated
  • people - Longing for reunion - Political maps versus lived experience - Borders unable to erase
  • language, customs and memories - New location without a sense of home - Disruption of cultural
  • continuity - Physical, emotional and cultural consequences of displacement - Lasting effects of
  • Partition; longing for reunion beyond borders.
  • / [CO2]

questions.question: "Toba Tek Singh" is deeply rooted in the specific history of the Partition, yet the story has resonated far beyond that moment and context. Discuss Manto's achievement in creating a story that is simultaneously a historical document and a universal meditation on borders, displacement, and belonging.
questions.solution_html:
• Saadat Hasan Manto; Partition of India - Exchange of asylum inmates between India and Pakistan -
  • Division of the subcontinent; political absurdity - Mental asylum as a miniature of the divided
  • subcontinent - Bishan Singh’s repeated question about Toba Tek Singh - Attachment to birthplace,
  • memory and identity - Confusion over national boundaries - Personal belonging versus political
  • classification - Fractured speech and confusion among inmates - Irrationality of political decisions
  • -“Sane” authorities versus “mad” inmates - Criticism of state power and arbitrary divisions -
  • Bishan Singh in the no-man’s-land between India and Pakistan - Neither country; absence of
  • secure belonging - Ending as a symbol of displacement and exclusion - Specific historical context
  • of Partition - Universal themes of borders, identity, displacement and home - State-imposed
  • categories versus human experience - Relevance beyond 1947; forced migration and territorial
  • conflict - Human cost of artificial boundaries - Memory and belonging beyond political maps
  • / [CO3]
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: How does Khushwant Singh portray displacement in The Train to Pakistan? [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Mano Majra initially represents peaceful coexistence among religious communities. Displacement
  • connected to different aspects like- Historical disruption-Partition destroys the village’s traditional
  • harmony. Forced migration-Trains carrying dead bodies reveal the brutality of communal violence.
  • Loss of home- Refugees experience fear, uncertainty, and separation from familiar places.
  • Communal polarization-Religious identity replaces earlier bonds of friendship and peaceful co-
  • existence. Human suffering- Ordinary villagers become victims of political decisions and
  • collective hatred. The railway- symbol travel and connection- now a vehicle of death. Khushwant
  • Singh - displacement - physical uprooting and the destruction of social trust and human
  • relationships. / [CO4]
  • [15x2 = 30]
